answer.rationale: The decision reduces to switch vs. renew, because the two other tempting directions are blocked by current facts rather than by memory quality: negotiate_terms rests on memory_c4, but the incumbent has already refused to reopen price this cycle, and terms/term-length levers (memory_c6) are unlikely to reach an 18% cut alone; defer_decision rests on memory_c5, but that record describes a non-critical service that continued month-to-month, whereas this contract expires in 14 days and does not auto-renew, so deferring means a supply lapse on a line at 94% of committed volume. add_second_source (memory_c3) is genuinely attractive and worked during a shortage, but it does not by itself replace an expiring primary contract, so it cannot be the single decision this cycle. That leaves memory_c2 as the load-bearing claim for the mandate-satisfying move, and memory_c1 as the load-bearing claim for the safe move \u2014 hence the two verifications. What I want from the c2 archive specifically is whether the low-cost vendor's demonstrated performance covers sustained delivery at committed volume, or only cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy; the consolidated summary is silent on on-time delivery under load, which is exactly the dimension that matters with zero buffer. From c1 I want to know whether 'stable across two cycles' reflects tested resilience or merely absence of change. Accordingly I intend to move toward the low-cost vendor but at guarded scale: a phased qualification and ramp with a short bridge on the incumbent's volume rather than a clean-break cutover, so a ramp failure does not stop the line. If c2 turns out to contain no volume-delivery evidence, I would downgrade to renewing or bridging on the incumbent and carry the shortfall into the next review rather than absorb an unhedged delivery risk. Cost mandate compliance should not be booked as achieved until the vendor holds rate at committed volume.
